newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai villagers suffer in marathon protest.
newsitem.headline: Thai villagers suffer in marathon protest.

text.p: Stress, cold and diarrhoea have hit hundreds of impoverished Thai protesters who are camping outside Government House in the capital demanding social justice, relief officials said on Thursday.

The sick are among 10,000 villagers who streamed into Bangkok from northeast Thailand last Friday and vowed to remain in make-shift shelters on two roads flanking Government House until their demands were met.
"About 300 patients turn up for first aid daily," a nurse assigned to look after the villagers told Reuters.
She said more than 10,000 pills had been handed out daily to the sick.
"At least six people who suffered from stress have been experiencing psychiatric problems and two of them were sent to hospital for treatment," she added.
Some of the villagers, who also cook food on the streets, complain they face severe problems with water and toilet facilities.
The government has provided some mobile toilets but villagers said the facilities were inadequate.

"Hundreds of people have to line up for a few mobile toilets every morning and it is getting worse because a neighbouring turf club closed off its toilets to us," said Kamsaeng Meekratok, a protester from Khonkhaen province.
The club, near Government House, allowed the protesters to use its toilets for a while but has now posted a sign saying the facilities are closed for renovation.

"Maybe the villagers have already filled up its toilet and that has forced the club to shut it down," Kamsaeng said. But despite the hardships, the villagers have pledged to push ahead with their marathon protest.

Organised by a movement called the Assembly of the Poor, they want to be released from indebtedness to the state-owned Agriculture and Cooperatives Bank, higher prices for their tapioca and settlement of land disputes with the government.
The Assembly's delegates met Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh on Monday and have held several rounds of negotiations with government officials this week.
But there is no sign of an end to the dispute.

"The problems being discussed are complicated and it involves many state agencies and law. So we need some time to reach agreement," said Chingchai Mongkoltham, minister in the prime minister's office, who is chairing the talks.
